reference.source: Bradley and Daroff Neurology in Clinical Practice / GeneReviews
clinicalPearls: Characterised by painless muscle stiffness that is worst on initiating movement after rest and eases with repeated contraction, the classic warm-up phenomenon
Caused by mutations in the CLCN1 gene encoding the skeletal-muscle chloride channel, with a dominant form (Thomsen disease) and a generally more severe recessive form (Becker myotonia)
Becker myotonia often shows transient weakness at the start of forceful exercise that then resolves, and tends to have a later onset and more marked muscle hypertrophy
Affected individuals frequently have a well-developed, athletic muscular appearance despite the functional handicap of stiffness
Grip myotonia and percussion myotonia can be demonstrated at the bedside, and eyelid myotonia may follow sustained forced closure
Cold can accentuate stiffness but, unlike paramyotonia congenita, myotonia congenita characteristically improves rather than worsens with continued activity
Symptomatic relief is achieved with sodium-channel-blocking antimyotonic agents when stiffness is disabling
reference.pathophysiology: Myotonia congenita results from loss-of-function mutations in CLCN1, the gene encoding the skeletal-muscle voltage-gated chloride channel ClC-1. This channel carries most of the resting membrane conductance and normally stabilises the sarcolemma after an action potential. When chloride conductance is reduced, potassium that accumulates in the transverse tubules during activity depolarises the membrane more readily, producing runs of repetitive after-discharges experienced as delayed muscle relaxation, or myotonia. The autosomal dominant form reflects a dominant-negative effect on the dimeric channel, whereas the recessive form arises when both alleles are severely impaired, and the transient warm-up improvement reflects redistribution of ions with repeated activity.
additionalDifferentials: Brody myopathy presenting with exercise-induced stiffness
Rippling muscle disease and other non-dystrophic causes of stiffness
additionalInvestigations: Electromyography demonstrating myotonic discharges with their characteristic waxing and waning pattern
Serum creatine kinase, which may be mildly elevated
Short exercise electromyography protocol, with and without cooling, to distinguish it from paramyotonia congenita
Assessment to exclude myotonic dystrophy, including examination for multisystem features
Muscle biopsy only where the diagnosis remains unclear
redFlags: Cardiac conduction disturbance or systemic features suggesting myotonic dystrophy rather than a pure channelopathy
Progressive fixed weakness, which is not expected and points to an alternative diagnosis
Severe stiffness compromising airway, swallowing or safe mobility
Adverse response to depolarising neuromuscular blockade during anaesthesia
reference.prognosis: Myotonia congenita is a non-progressive, non-dystrophic disorder compatible with a normal lifespan, and although stiffness can be functionally limiting it often stabilises or improves in adulthood and usually responds to antimyotonic therapy.
pitfalls: Mistaking it for myotonic dystrophy and missing the systemic surveillance the latter requires, or vice versa
Confusing the warm-up phenomenon of myotonia congenita with the paradoxical cold-worsened myotonia of paramyotonia congenita
Overlooking the transient exercise-induced weakness of Becker myotonia and labelling it a fixed myopathy
Not warning about depolarising muscle relaxants and other anaesthetic triggers of severe myotonia
references: Bradley and Daroff Neurology in Clinical Practice
management: Relieve disabling stiffness with antimyotonic sodium-channel-blocking agents such as mexiletine, with lamotrigine or carbamazepine as alternatives
Advise on the warm-up phenomenon and gradual initiation of activity to reduce stiffness
Advise avoidance of cold exposure, which can accentuate the stiffness
Take anaesthetic precautions, avoiding depolarising muscle relaxants such as suxamethonium that provoke myotonia
Confirm the diagnosis with CLCN1 genetic testing and distinguish the dominant Thomsen from the recessive Becker form
Offer genetic counselling appropriate to the inheritance pattern
Reassure regarding the non-progressive course and normal lifespan
